steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the History section of the Wikipedia article on 4th Dimension (4D), the database software: how it started and why Apple did not publish it, the company behind it, and the main releases over the years.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Origins as Silver Surfer; Apple's cancelled publishing plan
- Independent publication and Apple's internal use
- ACI, ACIUS and 4D Inc.
- Major releases (1993–2010)

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Origins
  - "Silver Surfer" during early development; Laurent Ribardière, 1984
  - after negotiations with Ribardiere, Apple Inc. (formerly Apple Computer Inc) planned to publish it
  - Apple canceled: reportedly pressure from other potential database publishers -> Apple "brand" database would disadvantage third-party products
  - Apple then trying to ensure well-known publishers supported Macintosh
- Independent publication
  - project reverted to Ribardière; published 4th Dimension with French businesswoman Marylene Delbourg-Delphis
  - Apple supported the venture, used 4D extensively: fitness center management, CIM (Computer Integrated Manufacturing)
  - Apple 4D experts: Lance McAndrew (Cupertino headquarters), Andrew O'Donoghue (Ireland-based European manufacturing HQ; 4D app managed European Service Center administration)
- Company
  - installed base grew over next few years
  - publisher ACI set up US subsidiary ACIUS, initially led by Guy Kawasaki
  - 16 years as ACIUS up to 2000, then officially renamed 4D Inc.
- Releases
  - 1993: 4D Server v1.1 (client/server) with 4th Dimension v3.1
  - 1995: 4D v3.5 cross-platform, Microsoft Windows + Apple Macintosh since
  - 1997: 4D v6, first with fully integrated web server; 4D forms -> HTML on the fly using only 4D language
  - 2004: 4D 2004, standalone, client/server, web and SOA apps without changing code
  - 2008: 4D v11, SQL layer in database engine, native SQL in 4D language, connect to local or remote servers
  - 2010: 4D v12, execute PHP functions/scripts from 4D language; replication and synchronization commands; 64 bit 4D Server

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Silver Surfer, which was what it was called during early development, was developed by Laurent Ribardière in 1984. After negotiations with Ribardiere, the plan was that Apple Inc. (formerly Apple Computer Inc) would publish the software. But Apple canceled the plan, reportedly because of pressure from other potential database publishers who said that if Apple had their own "brand" database, third-party products would be at a disadvantage in the marketplace. At the time Apple was trying to make sure well-known software publishers supported the Macintosh platform. So the project went back to Laurent Ribardière, and he published 4th Dimension together with the French businesswoman Marylene Delbourg-Delphis. Even though it was published independently, Apple supported the new venture and used 4D a lot throughout the organization for projects like fitness center management and CIM (Computer Integrated Manufacturing). A number of people at Apple became 4D experts, for example Lance McAndrew in Apple's Cupertino headquarters and Andrew O'Donoghue in Apple's European manufacturing headquarters in Ireland, where a 4th Dimension application managed the administration of the European Service Center.

In the next few years the installed base of 4th Dimension grew, and the publisher ACI set up a subsidiary in the US called ACIUS, which was led at first by Guy Kawasaki. It operated as ACIUS for 16 years up to 2000, and then the name was officially changed to 4D Inc.

- Releases
  - 1993: 4D Server v1.1 (client/server) with 4th Dimension v3.1
  - 1995: 4D v3.5 cross-platform, Microsoft Windows + Apple Macintosh since
  - 1997: 4D v6, first with fully integrated web server; 4D forms -> HTML on the fly using only 4D language
  - 2004: 4D 2004, standalone, client/server, web and SOA apps without changing code
  - 2008: 4D v11, SQL layer in database engine, native SQL in 4D language, connect to local or remote servers
  - 2010: 4D v12, execute PHP functions/scripts from 4D language; replication and synchronization commands; 64 bit 4D Server

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Silver Surfer, which was what it was called during early development, was developed by Laurent Ribardière in 1984. After negotiations with Ribardiere, the plan was that Apple Inc. (formerly Apple Computer Inc) would publish the software. But Apple canceled the plan, reportedly because of pressure from other potential database publishers who said that if Apple had their own "brand" database, third-party products would be at a disadvantage in the marketplace. At the time Apple was trying to make sure well-known software publishers supported the Macintosh platform. So the project went back to Laurent Ribardière, and he published 4th Dimension together with the French businesswoman Marylene Delbourg-Delphis. Even though it was published independently, Apple supported the new venture and used 4D a lot throughout the organization for projects like fitness center management and CIM (Computer Integrated Manufacturing). A number of people at Apple became 4D experts, for example Lance McAndrew in Apple's Cupertino headquarters and Andrew O'Donoghue in Apple's European manufacturing headquarters in Ireland, where a 4th Dimension application managed the administration of the European Service Center.

In the next few years the installed base of 4th Dimension grew, and the publisher ACI set up a subsidiary in the US called ACIUS, which was led at first by Guy Kawasaki. It operated as ACIUS for 16 years up to 2000, and then the name was officially changed to 4D Inc.

In 1993 4D Server v1.1 was introduced, which was the client/server version of 4th Dimension, together with the release of 4th Dimension v3.1.

In 1995 4D v3.5 went cross-platform, and since then it has supported both the Microsoft Windows and Apple Macintosh operating systems.

In 1997 4D v6 was the first version of 4D with a fully integrated web server. Developers could translate 4D forms into HTML on the fly with only the 4D language.

In 2004 4D 2004 was the first version of 4D where developers could create standalone, client/server, web and Service Oriented Applications (SOA) without having to change any code.

In 2008 4D v11 added a SQL layer to the 4D database engine and extended native SQL into the 4D programming language, so 4D developers could write native SQL code to connect to local or remote servers.

In 2010 4D v12 added the ability to execute PHP functions/scripts from inside the 4D programming language. This version also supported new replication and synchronization commands and there was a 64 bit version of 4D Server.

## Version history

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Silver Surfer, as it was known during early development, was developed by Laurent Ribardière in 1984. Following negotiations with Ribardiere, it was planned that Apple Inc. (formerly Apple Computer Inc) would publish the software, but Apple canceled the plan, reportedly due to pressure from other potential database publishers who claimed that if Apple had their own "brand" database, third-party products would be disadvantaged in the marketplace.[1] Apple was trying at the time to ensure that well-known software publishers supported the Macintosh platform, and as a result the project reverted to Laurent Ribardière, who published 4th Dimension with the French businesswoman Marylene Delbourg-Delphis. Although it was independently published, Apple supported the new venture and used 4D extensively throughout the organization for projects including fitness center management and CIM (Computer Integrated Manufacturing). A number of Apple personnel became 4D experts, including Lance McAndrew in Apple's Cupertino headquarters and Andrew O'Donoghue in Apple's Ireland-based European manufacturing headquarters, where a 4th Dimension application managed the administration of the European Service Center.

Over the next few years the installed base of 4th Dimension grew, and the publisher ACI established a US-based subsidiary called ACIUS, initially led by Guy Kawasaki. After 16 years of operating as ACIUS up to 2000, the name was officially changed to 4D Inc.[2]

In 1993, 4D Server v1.1, the client/server version of 4th Dimension, was introduced along with the release of 4th Dimension v3.1.[3]

In 1995, 4D v3.5 went cross-platform and has since supported both the Microsoft Windows and Apple Macintosh operating systems.[4]

In 1997, 4D v6 was the first version of 4D to contain a fully integrated web server, allowing developers to translate 4D forms into HTML on the fly using only the 4D language.[5]

In 2004, 4D 2004 was the first version of 4D to let developers create standalone, client/server, web and Service Oriented Applications (SOA) without changing any code.[6]

In 2008, 4D v11 added a SQL layer to the 4D database engine and extended native SQL into the 4D programming language, which allowed 4D developers to write native SQL code to connect to either local or remote servers.[7,8]

In 2010, 4D v12 integrated the ability to execute PHP functions/scripts from within the 4D programming language. This version also supported new replication and synchronization commands and included a 64 bit version of 4D Server.[9]
